reader.title: Lynching of George Montgomery
bases: A vigilance committee hanged a captured man accused of horse stealing before seventy-five to one hundred men (A6); wire reports call it the lynching of horse thieves (A1, A5).

Montgomery was hanged by a citizens' 'vigilant committee' with no lawful authority, before seventy-five or one hundred men, as a horse thief (A6); wire reports agree that Kansas farmers hanged horse thieves in No Man's Land (A1, A5).

The Wichita Eagle account (A6) and the independent Woodward and Oklahoma specials (A1, A5) agree that Ashland-area vigilantes hanged horse thieves in No Man's Land that week, though they differ on the number; Montgomery's name appears only in A6.

summary.text: The lynching of George Montgomery was the hanging of a man accused of horse stealing by a vigilance committee of Kansas and No Man's Land settlers at Neutral City, No Man's Land, on Sunday, April 8, 1888.
According to an account carried by the Wichita Eagle, Montgomery was captured with four horses said to be stolen, was said to have confessed, and was hanged before seventy-five or one hundred men.
Wire specials from Woodward and Oklahoma, Indian Territory, instead told of Kansas farmers hanging four horse thieves and besieging the rest of their band, so the reports disagree on how many died.
In the spring of 1888 the neutral strip known as "No Man's Land" was described as a base for horse thieves who raided the border towns of southern Kansas.
Mr. Van Denburg, quoted by the Wichita Eagle, said that for two weeks "an organized band of horse thieves" had been running stock between Clark County, Kansas, and No Man's Land.
Citizens around Ashland and Englewood and settlers of No Man's Land then formed what he called a "vigilant committee" to break up the gang and raid its stronghold.
In the southwestern part of No Man's Land the vigilantes captured two "notorious horse thieves of the Chitwood gang" and George Montgomery, who was said to have four stolen horses.
The Eagle dated the capture to "Saturday, the 17th inst." and the hanging to "Sunday, the 8th," an unexplained inconsistency.
The prisoners were taken to Neutral City, where the vigilantes assembled and hanged Montgomery from a pole projecting from a shanty in the presence of seventy-five or one hundred men.
By the same account, he made a full confession naming the members of the gang and where the stolen stock was kept.
The two other captives were released on promises to return stolen stock, after first putting up good horses as a guarantee.
The vigilantes then moved in a body on the thieves' barricaded rendezvous, and Van Denburg predicted a bloody encounter.
Wire reports said the remaining thieves, nine by the Woodward count and six by the Oklahoma count, were held in the Cherokee Strip or in a dugout and would be hanged if caught.

A Wheeling Register brief reported that "several of the lynchers are under arrest" after a mob lynched horse thieves near "Hearaldtown," Indian Territory, but it named no victim and may describe another lynching.
No report of an inquest, indictment or trial for Montgomery's death was found.

Most papers learned of the hanging through a Kansas City Times special from Woodward, which ran from April 11 in the Omaha Daily Bee, the Stark County Democrat and the Emporia Weekly News and was condensed as late as April 27 in the Phillipsburg Herald.
Under headlines such as "Horse Lifters Lynched" and "Four Horse Thieves Lynched," this version named no one and reported without comment that forty farmers had "strung up four horse thieves."

An Oklahoma special gave a different version, linking the hangings to a fight near Shawneetown in which a deputy U.S. marshal and Indian police battled three "colored horse thieves," two of whom were killed.

The Los Angeles Daily Herald ran it as "Judge Lynch" over "Colored Outlaw's Strung Up in No-Man's-Land," while the True Northerner of Paw Paw, Michigan, described the farmers as "avengers" who "meted out summary justice to four horse-thieves."
The Omaha Daily Bee, by contrast, printed the Shawneetown fight as a separate item, "With Winchesters," with no tie to the hangings.
Only the Wichita Eagle, on April 13, named Montgomery, in an interview with Van Denburg that called the thieves "miserable wretches" and offered no criticism of the committee.
The number killed differs by source: the Eagle's account describes one man hanged at Neutral City, while the Woodward and Oklahoma specials report four horse thieves hanged.

The race of those hanged is also uncertain, since the Eagle gives none for Montgomery, while the Los Angeles headline calls the hanged "colored," a term the fuller Oklahoma text applies only to the men in the marshal's fight.
The Eagle's account alone gives a name, place and date, but it comes from the vigilantes' district and rests on their version of Montgomery's guilt.

accounts.label: Van Denburg's account (vigilantes' district)
accounts.gist: A vigilant committee from Ashland, Englewood and No Man's Land captured Montgomery and two Chitwood gang men, hanged Montgomery at Neutral City on Sunday the 8th after a confession, and released the other two.

accounts.label: Woodward special (Kansas City Times)
accounts.gist: Forty farmers from Ashland and other Kansas towns strung up four horse thieves in No Man's Land last week and had nine more barricaded in the Cherokee Strip.

accounts.label: Oklahoma special
accounts.gist: After a marshal's posse fought colored horse thieves near Shawneetown, about fifty farmers or ranchmen captured four of the band and hanged them to the nearest tree, besieging six more in a dugout.

accounts.label: Brief telegram
accounts.gist: A mob of citizens lynched a gang of horse thieves near 'Hearaldtown,' Indian Territory, and several lynchers were arrested.

framing.detail: 'Horse Lifters Lynched' and 'Four Horse Thieves Lynched' briefs repeat the Woodward special without comment.
'Judge Lynch / Colored Outlaw's Strung Up in No-Man's-Land' racializes the hanged band in the headline.
'Horse Thieves Lynched' calls the hanging 'summary justice' by 'avengers' against outlaws.
The Eagle relays Van Denburg's praise of the 'law-abiding people' backing the committee and calls the thieves 'miserable wretches.'

conflicts.note: A6 is the only account with a name, place and date and comes from the vigilantes' own district; the four-man figure comes from wire specials that also merge a separate posse fight.
The 17th cannot precede the 8th; the Eagle's date is internally inconsistent.
The fuller Oklahoma special (A8) applies 'colored' only to the three men in the marshal's fight; the Omaha Bee prints that fight as a separate story (A1).
Counts may describe the raiding party versus the crowd at the hanging.
A4 may describe this or another lynching.
